title: Impact of mood and neurocognitive diagnosis on California Verbal Learning Test intrusions, repetitions and recognition
abstract: Abstract Mood symptoms, including both depression and anxiety, have been shown to have differential patterns on neuropsychological test results. Specific patterns of mood impacting the outcomes of the California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT) have not been fully explored, especially as they may interact with cognitive diagnoses. This study analysed data from 402 adult participants across two sites who underwent outpatient neuropsychological assessment. Specific analyses included whether the interaction between depression symptomatology with cognitive diagnosis (no diagnosis, Mild Neurocognitive Disorder, or Major Neurocognitive Disorder) was associated with CVLT repetition, intrusions, recognition hits and recognition false positives covarying for age, gender, education and site. These analyses were then repeated for the interaction between anxiety symptomatology and cognitive diagnosis. Results identified patterns of predictability, with significant interactions between depression and cognitive diagnosis predicting intrusion errors ( β = −11.770, p < .001) and false positive errors ( β = −3.942, p = .006), such that significant depression symptoms and a cognitive diagnosis were associated with fewer intrusion and false positive errors. There were also main effects for depression predicting recognition hits ( β = −.664, p = .005), cognitive diagnosis predicting recognition hits ( β = −1.273, p < .001; β = −.813, p = .002) and anxiety predicting repetition errors ( β = −.896, p = .044). These results show potential patterns for clinicians to analyse in their patient populations to help differentiate whether cognitive diagnosis, mood symptomatology and/or an interaction between the two may be present for their patients.
